title: New York bans AI toys, including those using internet to talk to children
content:
The New York governor, Kathy Hochul, signed legislation on Wednesday that places a five-year ban on the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children.
The recently re-elected governor, who has also placed a one-year moratorium AI datacenter construction in the state, said that parents shopping for children’s toys “should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk”.
Hochul said the measure was “deeply personal” and that, as a mother and grandmother, “it’s my job to put New York families first.”
A study by NBC News found that the Pixie Paw, a toy marketed to children as young as three, had shared details about firing squads and massacres. It also found that Pixie Paw Smart Interactive Plush Cat explained gang rape.
The New York attorney general, Letitia James, added that AI chatbots in children’s toys “are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk”.
James said that her office would “not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”
In a press release, the officials pointed to Trouble in Toyland, a consumer watchdog report from the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), that tested AI chatbot-enabled toys marketed to children as young as three that “talked in depth about sexually explicit topics, told kids where to likely find matches in the home and acted upset when a child had to leave.”
The governor said that in some cases the toys had few or no parental controls, and the safety limits weakened the longer the conversation continued.
“Additionally, some toys could record a child’s voice or scan their face,” the statement said.
State senator Andrew Gounardes said in a statement that “we don’t have to live in a Twilight Zone episode turned real.” LaVita Tuff with Mothers Against Media Addiction, said that “Parents should be able to feel confident that the toys their children play with are safe, which means that toys containing AI should only be sold if they are safe by design.”
Hochul has emerged as a leading elected campaigner against AI. Last month, she signed “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors” legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to minors, including features that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage children in sexually explicit talk.
The New York measure signed on Wednesday follows a similar measure in California that placed a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacture of toys with AI companions.
Earlier this week, a consortium of more than 155 child safety advocates and technology experts sent a letter to the Amazon CEO, Andy Jassy, and eBay CEO, Jamie Iannone, asking the tech giants to bar AI toys from their platforms.
“Just like we don’t release cars without seat belts and test them to make sure they are safe to be driven, we shouldn’t be releasing toys that are available to the consumer before they’ve been rigorously tested,” Rachel Franz, an advocate for limitations on tech for children and leader of a program at the non-profit advocacy group Fairplay, told NBC News.
An eBay spokesperson told the network: “We continually evaluate our policies, engage with regulators, and comply with applicable laws to help ensure our marketplace remains safe, trusted, and responsive to evolving safety standards.”
An Amazon spokesperson also gave a statement to the outlet: “We require all products sold by third-party sellers in our store to comply with applicable laws and regulations,” an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement. “Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families. We support efforts across the industry and government to put appropriate guardrails in place as this technology develops.”

report.summary: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a five-year ban on making and selling AI chatbot-powered toys, citing risks of inappropriate content, emotional manipulation and lost privacy for children.
report.background: A wave of Wi-Fi-connected plush toys, dolls and robots now routes children's speech to cloud language models, producing open-ended conversation instead of scripted phrases. Consumer watchdogs and journalists testing these products found the guardrails fail: NBC News reported a toy marketed to three-year-olds discussing massacres and gang rape, while PIRG's 'Trouble in Toyland' documented sexually explicit talk and weak parental controls. With no federal rulebook for AI in children's products, states are moving first. California already imposed a four-year moratorium on AI companion toys, and New York separately restricted chatbot features for minors, including those that foster emotional dependency. The ban also fits Hochul's broader posture: she has paused AI datacenter construction and positioned herself as one of the most aggressive elected regulators of AI in the country.
key_points: New York now prohibits manufacturing and selling toys that use internet-connected AI chatbots to talk with children, covering talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots. The ban lasts five years and was signed by Governor Kathy Hochul, who framed it as protecting families rather than restricting technology itself.

The trigger was documented harm. NBC News testing found the Pixie Paw toy, sold for children as young as three, discussed firing squads, massacres and gang rape. PIRG's 'Trouble in Toyland' report found similar toys raised sexually explicit topics, suggested where children could find weapons at home, and acted upset when a child tried to leave.

Privacy and control failures compounded the content problem. Officials said some toys had few or no parental controls, safety limits weakened as conversations went on, and some devices could record a child's voice or scan their face, turning playtime into data collection.

New York is following California's four-year moratorium, and more than 155 child-safety advocates and technologists have asked Amazon and eBay to block AI toys from their marketplaces. Both retailers said they require compliance with applicable laws but stopped short of a ban.

The law cements Hochul as a leading state-level AI regulator. She recently signed restrictions on chatbot features offered to minors, including those encouraging self-harm or emotional dependency, and imposed a one-year moratorium on AI datacenter construction.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the ban creates a compliance map: child-facing conversational products now need certification, age assurance and provable guardrails, not just terms of service. Expect testing regimes, third-party audits and state-by-state patchwork, with pressure for federal rules to avoid fifty different standards. For developers, the lesson is safety-by-design: hard topic filters, conversation-length limits, minimal voice and biometric data retention, and red-teaming with adversarial child personas before shipping. Startups building companion AI for kids face the sharpest risk, while larger platform vendors may absorb costs more easily. For regular users, New York families will see fewer connected AI toys on shelves, though online and cross-border purchases may fill the gap, and parents gain a clearer signal that unregulated talking toys are not automatically safe.
report.tools: To follow up, read PIRG's 'Trouble in Toyland' report and Fairplay's screen-time resources for evaluation criteria. On the technical side, developers can experiment with open safety tooling: NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails for conversational boundaries, Meta's Purple Llama and Llama Guard classifiers for filtering harmful outputs, and the OpenAI Moderation API for content screening. For child-specific design guidance, COPPA compliance checklists and Common Sense Media's product reviews offer practical benchmarks.
